title: Elephants in gold
hookLine: drunken elephants decked in gold, horses swift as deer, kings in glory, and all leave this world empty-handed (Savaiye 2)

lines: KINGS, AND ROWS OF BOWED HEADS.
cards: The parade comes down the road and the crowd goes quiet. First the elephants, huge and swaying, drunk on their own strength, hung with gold that flashes in the sun.
Then the horses, thousands of them, quick as deer, barely touching the ground. Then the kings, broad in the shoulder, with rows of people bowing their heads on either side. Nobody can look away.
And the poet leans over and whispers one question.

teach.b: That's the second savaiya. In paraphrase: maddened elephants decked in gold, tall and matchless. Horses by the million, leaping like deer, outrunning the wind.
Mighty kings before whom countless heads bow. Then the question: and what of it?

teach.h: AT THE END, THEY LEFT BAREFOOT.
teach.b: Such great kings there have been, and at the end they went away barefoot. In the Guru's world, a king never walked anywhere. He rode.
So the one who arrived on an elephant leaves on his own bare feet, carrying nothing, empty-handed, the way everyone leaves. What keeps this from easy moralizing is the man writing it.
Guru Gobind Singh knew this world from the inside. He held court at Anandpur. He rode fine horses, and Sikh tradition tells of an elephant called Prasadi, brought to the young Guru as a gift.

teach.h: THE GURU KNEW THE GOLD UP CLOSE.
teach.b: He'd seen the gold up close and knew what it could and couldn't do. Notice what the verse doesn't say.

teach.h: NOT A BAN ON BEAUTIFUL THINGS.
teach.b: It doesn't call elephants evil or beautiful things wrong; Sikhs aren't asked to give up their homes or their work.
It simply follows the parade to its end, past the city gates, to the last walk every king takes, where the gold stays behind. It doesn't say here what should be carried instead.
It leaves the question standing at the gate: if not the gold, then what?

how: Many Sikhs recite this as the second of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning; it is often explained as a reminder that wealth and power stay behind when a person dies.

kings before whom many heads bow

games.q: elephants in gold — tap the pairs.

s: the second savaiya says owning beautiful things is a sin
it doesn't ban anything. it follows the parade to its end, where the gold stays behind.
the verse pictures the kings leaving barefoot
a king always rode. at the end he walks out on his own bare feet, carrying nothing.
Guru Gobind Singh wrote this as a poor man who never saw a court
he held court at Anandpur, rode fine horses, and tradition tells of an elephant gifted to him.

games.q: the great kings ride past on elephants hung with gold, and countless heads bow. the poet asks: and what of it? how does the verse answer?
o: at the end, they went away barefoot.
games.why: such great kings there have been, and at the end they left barefoot. a king never walked; now he walks out with nothing.

practice: Pick up one thing you own, a watch, a mug, a ring, and really look at it: where it came from, what it's been through with you.
Enjoy it honestly, without guilt, and let a second, light thought sit beside the first: one day it won't be yours. Smile at it the way you'd smile at a friend you know you'll part from one day.

wordCard.voice: Maate matang, maddened elephants. The second savaiya's parade of power: elephants, horses and bowing heads, and kings who still left this world barefoot.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: maate matang, maddened elephants, the opening words of the second savaiya.

carryVoice: Your line: they left empty-handed. The gold stays at the gate. See you at the next verse.

sources.work: Sikh historical tradition (e.g., Bhai Santokh Singh, Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth)
